body:
Embroidery as a regional and community tradition

Embroidery decorates a fabric by adding stitches after the base textile has been prepared. Its patterns may be formed with coloured threads and may incorporate mirrors, beads or other attached ornaments.

Kutch is especially important for the variety of its embroidery traditions. Different communities have developed characteristic combinations of motifs, colours, stitches and uses.

Traditional embroidery has adorned garments, quilts, household textiles and bridal trousseaus. Because garments were worn during particular social occasions, embroidery could also communicate community identity and customary status.

Major embroidery traditions of Kutch

Tradition or communityRecognisable association
Rabari embroideryPastoral community traditions; bold decorative forms and frequent use of mirrors
Ahir embroideryColourful ornamental designs associated with Ahir community textiles
Jat embroideryDense geometrical patterns, often with small mirrors in traditional examples
Mutava embroideryFine decorative needlework and small-scale ornamentation
Suf or Soof embroideryCounted-thread geometrical designs constructed through triangular forms

The table identifies broad associations. It does not imply that every textile belonging to a community must use the same colours or motifs. Artistic traditions vary between families, settlements and periods.

Suf embroidery: a distinctive geometric tradition

Suf embroidery is particularly associated with Kutch. Its design vocabulary is built around the triangle, and its symmetrical patterns are developed by counting the threads of the fabric.

Traditional Suf work is stitched from the reverse of the cloth without first drawing the complete design on its surface. This gives the craft a recognisable geometrical character.

Suf embroidery is still embroidery, even though the artisan counts warp and weft threads. The counting helps to position the stitches; it does not turn the work into a woven pattern.

Gujarat Suf Embroidery appears as a registered geographical indication in the official GI register.

Tangaliya: raised dots made during weaving

Tangaliya is a distinctive weaving tradition associated especially with Surendranagar district in Saurashtra. It has been practised by the Dangasia weaving community.

Its characteristic raised dots are known as daana. These are created through additional yarn inserted and manipulated during weaving, producing textured geometric designs.

Traditionally, Tangaliya textiles were closely associated with woollen shawls and garments used by pastoral communities. Contemporary production also includes other materials and articles for wider markets.

The essential distinction is that Tangaliya's raised decoration is formed on the loom. It may resemble bead embroidery, but it is not simply embroidery stitched onto finished fabric.

Kachchh shawls and pastoral livelihoods

Kachchh shawls are associated with the weaving heritage of Kutch. The region's pastoral economy historically supported the use of wool in blankets, shawls and other garments.

Traditional communities used locally available fibres and developed textiles suited to the climate and customary clothing requirements. Decorative borders and motifs helped give these products a recognisable regional identity.

Centres such as Bhujodi are associated with the continuing weaving heritage of Kutch. Contemporary production includes shawls and other articles adapted for broader markets.

Bharuch Sujani: quilting created on the loom

Sujani weaving of Bharuch produces a distinctive padded, quilt-like textile.

Its principal characteristic is the construction of 2 interwoven layers of cloth, with spaces that can be filled with cotton during the weaving process. The fabric develops a characteristic checked or compartmented appearance.

This is different from the more familiar method of making a quilt by stitching together separate fabric layers around padding. The structure of Bharuch Sujani is principally created by the weaving itself.

The tradition illustrates how a handloom can produce not just a flat decorative cloth but a functional padded textile.

Comparisons with other Indian embroidery traditions

Several major embroidery traditions outside Gujarat provide useful points of comparison.

TraditionRegionMain association
PhulkariPunjabBrightly coloured embroidery; floral and ornamental tradition
KanthaBengalRunning-stitch decoration, often associated with layered textiles
ChikankariLucknow, Uttar PradeshDelicate embroidery, frequently floral
KasutiKarnatakaGeometrical and pictorial embroidery
Pipli appliquéOdishaAttached coloured fabric shapes; historically associated with ceremonial textiles

These forms may share broad materials or decorative purposes, but their regional names and characteristic methods remain distinct.

Why local craft names are important

The names Tangaliya, Suf embroidery, Kachchh shawls and Bharuch Sujani refer to different products. A question that identifies a craft merely as a textile from Gujarat has not provided enough information to distinguish them.

The decisive clues are whether the pattern is stitched after weaving, formed as raised dots during weaving, or created through a special woven fabric structure.

Prelims focus

  • Kutch: Rabari, Ahir, Jat and other community embroidery traditions.
  • Suf: geometrical counted-thread embroidery based on triangular forms.
  • Tangaliya: Surendranagar; Dangasia community; raised daana dots made during weaving.
  • Kachchh shawls: regional weaving heritage of Kutch.
  • Bharuch Sujani: padded double-cloth textile formed through weaving.
  • Phulkari: Punjab; Kantha: Bengal; Chikankari: Lucknow.
  • Trap: Tangaliya's raised dots are woven, whereas Kutch mirror embroidery is added by stitching.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class XI, 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–14, and 'Textiles', printed pp. 92–96; District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, 'Handicraft', section 'The Main Styles of Embroidery in Kachchh', including Suf, accessed 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, 'Tangaliya', Surendranagar, accessed 23 November 2026; National Institute of Fashion Technology, 'Soof Embroidery', Cluster Studies project, accessed 23 November 2026; Ministry of Textiles, 'Sustainability in the Handloom Traditions of India', sections 'Sujani Fabrics', p. 39, and 'Tangaliya', p. 41; Intellectual Property India, GI application details for Bharuch Sujani Weaving, application 1090, and state-wise registered GI list, applications 103, 127, 174 and 997, data as of 31 December 2025.]

body:
Why the raw material matters

The physical properties of a material influence what an artisan can make. Clay can be shaped while moist and hardened by firing. Metals can be shaped or cast to produce durable objects. Wood can be carved, turned and decorated. Stone can be cut and polished. Fibres and yarns can be interlaced to make flexible textiles.

Craft identification therefore often begins with the relationship between material, product and place.

Clay and terracotta

Pottery is the making of objects from prepared clay, generally followed by drying and firing. Clay vessels may be used for storing water, cooking, carrying food or performing ceremonies.

Terracotta literally refers to fired earth and commonly describes unglazed fired-clay objects. Traditional terracotta crafts include figurines, toys, decorative panels and ritual objects as well as useful household articles.

Gujarat has important pottery traditions, including those associated with Khavda in Kutch and terracotta work in other districts. Traditional decoration reflects local preferences and available materials.

Clay objects are also important in ritual life. Earthen pots may appear in marriage customs, household ceremonies and the celebration of festivals.

A pottery object may be decorative or functional, and a terracotta figure may be religious or secular. Its material alone does not determine its cultural purpose.

Metal crafts and alloys

Traditional metalworking has produced utensils, bells, ornaments, tools, sculptures and objects used in religious ceremonies.

Some useful distinctions are based on the composition of the metal:

MaterialComposition or propertyCommon craft use
BrassAlloy of copper and zincUtensils, decorative objects and fittings
BronzePrincipally copper and tinCast objects, sculpture and traditional utensils
Bell metalCopper-tin alloy, generally with a relatively high tin contentBells and certain traditional vessels
IronStrong, workable metalTools, implements and structural components

One traditional method of producing metal figures is lost-wax casting. A model is formed in wax and covered with mould material. Heating removes the wax, leaving space for molten metal. When the metal solidifies, the mould is removed to reveal the cast object.

This broad principle is associated with several regional metal-casting traditions, including Dhokra work in parts of central and eastern India.

Copper-coated bells of Kutch

Nirona in Kutch is also associated with a traditional metal-bell craft. The bells were historically used with livestock and are now produced for decorative and other purposes.

Despite the name copper bell, the object is not necessarily made from solid copper. Traditional work commonly involves a shaped metal body with a copper-containing surface treatment.

This distinction matters because the commercial name of a craft does not always identify the complete material composition of the object.

Wood crafts: Sankheda, Pethapur and Surat

Sankheda furniture

Sankheda furniture is associated with Sankheda in the Chhota Udepur region of Gujarat, near Vadodara. Its traditional practitioners include artisans of the Kharadi community.

The craft combines turned wooden forms, painted ornamentation and a lacquered finish. Furniture, cradles, swings, stools and related household products are among its recognised forms.

The characteristic appearance depends on both the shaping of wood and its decorative surface. Sankheda furniture is therefore a woodworking and lacquer-decoration tradition, not a textile craft.

Pethapur printing blocks

Pethapur, near Gandhinagar, is known for carved wooden blocks used in textile printing.

The artisan produces the printing tool by carving the design into wood. A textile printer subsequently uses that block to apply patterns to cloth.

Thus, the block maker and the textile printer carry out connected but different craft activities. Pethapur Printing Blocks is a registered geographical indication in its own right.

Surat Sadeli

Sadeli is a decorative inlay or marquetry tradition associated with Surat. Small pieces of material are arranged into intricate geometrical patterns on a surface, particularly on wooden objects.

Its products include decorative boxes and other articles. Sadeli differs from wood-block printing because the small pieces form a permanent inlaid design on the object rather than a printing tool for transferring a design to cloth.

Stone and jewellery crafts

Agates of Cambay

Cambay is the historical English name for Khambhat in Gujarat. The town is associated with the cutting, shaping and polishing of agate, a variety of microcrystalline quartz.

Agates occur in different colours and patterns. Artisans produce beads, jewellery and decorative objects by shaping and polishing suitable stones.

Agates of Cambay is a registered geographical indication. The craft is distinguished by its association with worked semiprecious stone, not by metal casting or textile dyeing.

Jewellery as a craft tradition

Traditional Indian jewellery may use precious metals, silver, beads, semiprecious stones and other materials. Jewellery can be ornamental, a store of wealth or a marker of community identity and ceremonial status.

Kutch and other regions of Gujarat have distinctive jewellery traditions associated with pastoral and other communities. As with embroidery, ornaments may communicate information about customary dress and social identity.

Material and craft-centre comparison

Craft centre or traditionMain materialPrincipal product
Khavda, KutchClayPottery
Nirona, KutchMetalTraditional copper-coated bells
SankhedaWood and lacquerDecorated furniture
PethapurWoodTextile-printing blocks
Surat SadeliSmall inlay materials and woodDecorative inlaid objects
KhambhatAgate stoneBeads and jewellery

Prelims focus

  • Brass: copper and zinc; bronze: principally copper and tin.
  • Lost-wax casting: wax model, mould and replacement by molten metal.
  • Sankheda: painted and lacquered wooden furniture.
  • Pethapur: carved blocks used for textile printing.
  • Surat Sadeli: decorative inlay or marquetry.
  • Cambay or Khambhat: agate craft.
  • Trap: A copper-coated bell need not be made entirely from copper.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class XI, 'Clay', printed pp. 15–19, 'Metal', printed pp. 37–42, and 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–14; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, 'Visit Nirona in Kutch', section 'Copper Bell Art', 'Pethapur Printing Blocks', and 'Agates of Cambay', accessed 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, 'Sankheda Furniture', and 'Niche Tourism', regional handicraft listings, accessed 23 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, state-wise registered GI list, entries for Sankheda Furniture, Agates of Cambay, Pethapur Printing Blocks and Surat Sadeli Craft, data as of 31 December 2025.]
